newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Afghan Taleban battle foes north of Kabul.
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban battle foes north of Kabul.

text.p: Afghan opposition forces launched counter-attacks against the Taleban militia north of Kabul early on Wednesday, a Pakistan-based news service said.

The Afghan Islamic Press (AIP) said guerrillas loyal to former government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood had fought their way back into the northern part of the vital town of Jabal-os-Siraj, 70 km (44 miles) from Kabul.
But the Taleban, who captured Jabal-os-Siraj on Tuesday, were still holding most of the town and the nearby village of Golbahar at the entrance to Masood's Panjsher Valley stronghold.
AIP said Masood's men had launched a separate attack to try to regain positions they lost on Tuesday in the village of Pul-i-Matak, a few km (miles) south of Jabal-os-Siraj.
Fighting was also raging about five km (three miles) east of Golbahar, the agency said.
It quoted Taleban sources as saying the purist Islamic militia had captured 100 opposition fighters in Tuesday's battles, most of them in Golbahar.
Opposition spokesmen could not immediately be reached for comment.

In a separate development, an ammunition dump blew up in the Bala Hisar district of Kabul, AIP reported. It quoted Taleban officials as saying there had been no casualties in the early morning blast. It was not clear what had caused the explosion.

The Taleban, who seized Kabul in September, launched a big offensive on Tuesday to recapture Golbahar and Jabal-os-Siraj, which straddles the main highway linking the Afghan capital to the north via the Salang Pass across the Hindu Kush mountains.

Masood had taken the two towns on Friday, cutting off a Taleban force that moved north of the Hindu Kush last week in an effort to link up with Taleban fighters who had established a fleeting presence in the northern capital of Mazar-i-Sharif.

They were expelled from Mazar-i-Sharif last Wednesday after heavy street fighting with an opposition Shi'ite Moslem militia backed by ethnic Uzbek troops who had previously allied with the Taleban against opposition warlord General Abdul Rashid Dostum.
The mainly ethnic Pashtun Taleban, still the largest single force in Afghanistan, want to impose their strict interpretation of Islamic sharia law throughout the war-shattered country.
